cards.title: Introduction to Functions
cards.content:
A function is a block of organized, reusable code that is used to perform a single, related action. Functions provide better modularity for your application and a high degree of code reusing.

In Python, a function is defined using the def keyword.

def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

cards.title: Parameters vs Arguments
cards.content:
Information can be passed into functions as arguments. Parameters are specified after the function name, inside the parentheses.

# x and y are parameters
def add(x, y):
    return x + y

# 5 and 3 are arguments
result = add(5, 3)

cards.title: *args and **kwargs
cards.content:
Sometimes you do not know how many arguments that will be passed into your function. You can use *args and **kwargs to handle variable numbers of arguments.

*args passes non-keyworded arguments as a tuple, while **kwargs passes keyworded arguments as a dictionary.

pairs.right: Keyword to exit function and pass back a value

cards.title: Lambda Functions
cards.content:
A lambda function is a small anonymous function. A lambda function can take any number of arguments, but can only have one expression.

x = lambda a : a + 10
print(x(5))  # Outputs: 15

Call the function by its name followed by parentheses
Receive and process the return value

cards.title: Variable Scope
cards.content:
A variable is only available from inside the region it is created. This is called scope.

  • Local Scope: Variables created inside a function.
  • Global Scope: Variables created in the main body of the Python code.

options.text: Local variables can be accessed anywhere in the file.
Global variables are only accessible inside functions.
Local variables are created inside a function and only accessible there.
There is no difference between local and global scope.

cards.title: Summary
cards.content:
You have learned the fundamentals of Python functions:

  • Defining functions with def
  • Passing arguments and using default values
  • Handling variable arguments with *args and **kwargs
  • Using anonymous lambda functions
  • Understanding variable scope
